'''Serena DeBeer''' (born 1973) is an American chemist. She is currently a W3-Professor and the director at the [[Max Planck Institute for Chemical Energy Conversion]] in [[Mülheim|Muelheim an der Ruhr]], [[Germany]], where she heads the Department of Inorganic Spectroscopy. Her expertise lies in the application and development of [[X-ray spectroscopy|X-ray based spectroscopic]] methods as probes of [[electronic structure]] in biological and chemical [[catalysis]].

== Education and career ==
Serena DeBeer studied at [[Southwestern University]], [[Georgetown, Texas|Georgetown]], Texas (US), where she completed her [[Bachelor's degree|bachelor]] program in [[chemistry]], with minor in [[mathematics]] in 1995 (with honors). She received her doctorate from [[Stanford University]] in 2002, working under the guidance of [[Edward I. Solomon]] and [[Keith Hodgson|Keith O. Hodgson]]. She then moved to [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory]], where she worked first as a beamline scientist (2001–2003) at the [[Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource|Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Laboratory]], and later as staff scientist (2003–2009). In the Fall of 2009, she relocated to [[Cornell University]] in [[Ithaca, New York|Ithaca, NY]] (USA), where she accepted a faculty position as [[assistant professor]] at the department of chemistry and chemical biology.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://chemistry.cornell.edu/serena-debeer |title = Serena DeBeer &#124; Chemistry & Chemical Biology Cornell Arts & Sciences}}</ref> In the Summer of 2011, she moved to Germany and started to work as a W2-Professor and research group leader at the Max Planck Institute for Bioinorganic Chemistry (since 2012 [[Max Planck Institute for Chemical Energy Conversion|Max Planck Institute for Chemical Energy Conversion, MPI CEC]]) in [[Mülheim|Mülheim an der Ruhr]], Germany. Since 2012 she has held the position of an adjunct professor at [[Cornell University]] as well as an honorary faculty position at [[Ruhr University Bochum]] since 2014.<ref name="rub">{{Cite web|url=https://news.rub.de/leute/2017-03-13-max-planck-institut-honorarprofessorin-der-rub-ist-neue-direktorin|title=Honorarprofessorin der RUB ist neue Direktorin|website=news.rub.de|date=13 March 2017 |language=de|access-date=2019-08-08}}</ref> DeBeer headed the research group "X-ray Spectroscopy" at MPI CEC until 2017 when she was appointed director at this institute and promoted to a W3-Professor. Currently she leads the department of "Inorganic Spectroscopy"<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cec.mpg.de/1/research/1087/prof-dr-serena-debeer/|title=Prof. Dr. Serena DeBeer|website=cec.mpg.de|access-date=2019-12-02}}</ref> at MPI CEC. Additionally, she is the group leader of the PINK beamline<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.helmholtz-berlin.de/projects/emil/instruments/analytics/pink_en.html|title=PINK|last=Energie|first=Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin für Materialien und|website=HZB Website|language=en-GB|access-date=2019-12-02}}</ref> project at the Energy and Materials In-Situ Laboratory<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://www.helmholtz-berlin.de/forschung/quellen/corelabs/emil/index_en.html|title=Energy Materials In-Situ Laboratory Berlin|last=Energie|first=Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin für Materialien und|website=HZB Website|language=en-GB|access-date=2019-12-02}}</ref> at the [[Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin|Helmholtz Zentrum Berlin]], Germany. Since 2024, Serena has held an honorary faculty position at [[University of Duisburg-Essen|University Duisburg-Essen]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=RSS-Beitrag |url=https://www.uni-due.de/apps/rss.php?db=chemie&id=2015101120 |access-date=2024-05-27 |website=www.uni-due.de}}</ref>

== Research ==
Research in the DeBeer group focuses on answering fundamental questions in energy research. Namely, how does one reversibly store and release energy from chemical bonds using earth abundant transition metals? And how is this done most efficiently? Her research group studies homogeneous, heterogeneous and biological catalysts in order to answer these questions, with a primary focus on enzymatic catalysis. She is an expert in the application of advanced X-ray spectroscopy to understand catalytic transformations.

===Nitrogenase===
A strong focus of her research is to study the enzyme that is responsible for the conversion of [[Nitrogen|dinitrogen]] (N<sub>2</sub>) to [[ammonia]] (NH<sub>3</sub>)—[[Nitrogenase]]. Serena DeBeer and her group study this remarkable system comprising a [[FeMoco|FeMo cofactor]] (FeMoco) as its active site, and structural model complexes utilizing high-resolution [[X-ray absorption spectroscopy|X-ray absorption]] (XAS) and [[X-ray emission spectroscopy]] (XES). Through this work, great progress has been made in understanding the structure of this active site. A key contribution was a spectroscopic identification of the central atom in the active site as a carbide.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Lancaster|first1=K. === Methane monooxygenase ===
Another important chemical conversion studied by her group is the catalytic oxidation of [[methane]] to [[methanol]]. Nature utilizes a group of enzymes called [[methane monooxygenase]] (MMOs). The active site of this enzyme that enables the cleavage of the C-H of [[methane]] is a dinuclear Fe(IV) intermediate Q found in the hydroxylase protein (MMOH) of MMO. Spectroscopic studies in the DeBeer group have provided new insights into the structure of this diiron complex. Through applications of advanced X-ray spectroscopic studies like high-resolution [[X-ray absorption spectroscopy|XAS]] they characterized the key intermediate in biological methane oxidation as an open-core diiron structure (with Fe<sup>IV</sup>=O motif).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Castillo|first1=Rebeca G.|last2=Banerjee|first2=Rahul|last3=Allpress|first3=Caleb J.|last4=Rohde|first4=Gregory T.|last5=Bill|first5=Eckhard|last6=Que|first6=Lawrence|last7=Lipscomb|first7=John D.|last8=DeBeer|first8=Serena|date=2017-12-13|title=High-Energy-Resolution Fluorescence-Detected X-ray Absorption of the Q Intermediate of Soluble Methane Monooxygenase|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|language=en|volume=139|issue=49|pages=18024–18033|doi=10.1021/jacs.7b09560|pmid=29136468|pmc=5729100|issn=0002-7863}}</ref> Additional [[Extended X-ray absorption fine structure|EXAFS]] studies confirmed this finding by showing no evidence for a short Fe-Fe distance but rather a long diiron distance consistent with an open-core structure.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cutsail|first1=George E.|last2=Banerjee|first2=Rahul|last3=Zhou|first3=Ang|last4=Que|first4=Lawrence|last5=Lipscomb|first5=John D.|last6=DeBeer|first6=Serena|date=2018-12-05|title=High-Resolution Extended X-ray Absorption Fine Structure Analysis Provides Evidence for a Longer Fe···Fe Distance in the Q Intermediate of Methane Monooxygenase|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|language=en|volume=140|issue=48|pages=16807–16820|doi=10.1021/jacs.8b10313|pmid=30398343|pmc=6470014|issn=0002-7863}}</ref>

=== Spectroscopy Development ===
Recent work of DeBeer's group has focused on developing the full information content of various X-ray spectroscopic methods and their application to biological catalysts.

Among these methods are:

==== Valence X-ray Emission Spectroscopy  ====
In this method (also known as VtC XES = Valence-to-Core X-ray Emission Spectroscopy), one monitors the resultant fluorescence after a valence electron refills the ionized metal 1s core hole. As such, valence XES spectra provide a map of ligand ionization energies, and provides information on both ligand identity and protonation state. A prominent application of this method its use to identify the central carbon atom in FeMo cofactor of Nitrogenase  (see section [[#Nitrogenase|Nitrogenase]]).<ref name=":0" />

==== Resonant valence XES (RXES) or Resonant Inelastic X-ray Scattering (RIXS) ====
The DeBeer group is actively involved in the development and application of RXES/[[Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering|RIXS]] based methods in both the hard and soft [[X-ray]] regime. These include 1s-Valence [[Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering|RIXS]] as a means to obtain ligand-selective [[X-ray absorption spectroscopy|XAS]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hall|first1=Eleanor R.|last2=Pollock|first2=Christopher J.|last3=Bendix|first3=Jesper|last4=Collins|first4=Terrence J.|last5=Glatzel|first5=Pieter|last6=DeBeer|first6=Serena|date=2014-07-16|title=Valence-to-Core-Detected X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy: Targeting Ligand Selectivity|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|language=en|volume=136|issue=28|pages=10076–10084|doi=10.1021/ja504206y|pmid=24946007|issn=0002-7863}}</ref> and 2p3d [[Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering|RIXS]] as a means to map out the d-d ==== X-ray Magnetic Circular Dichroism (XMCD) ====
This method has been extensively used in solid-state materials, to determine the magnetic properties. Past applications to (bio-)inorganic or protein systems were lacking proper qualitative and quantitative interpretations. DeBeer's group expanded the information that can be obtained from XMCD of covalent systems.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kowalska|first1=Joanna K.|last2=Nayyar|first2=Brahamjot|last3=Rees|first3=Julian A.|last4=Schiewer|first4=Christine E.|last5=Lee|first5=Sonny C.|last6=Kovacs|first6=Julie A.|last7=Meyer|first7=Franc|last8=Weyhermüller|first8=Thomas|last9=Otero|first9=Edwige|last10=DeBeer|first10=Serena|date=2017-07-17|title=Iron L 2,3 -Edge X-ray Absorption and X-ray Magnetic Circular Dichroism Studies of Molecular Iron Complexes with Relevance to the FeMoco and FeVco Active Sites of Nitrogenase|journal=Inorganic Chemistry|language=en|volume=56|issue=14|pages=8147–8158|doi=10.1021/acs.inorgchem.7b00852|issn=0020-1669|pmc=5516708|pmid=28653855}}</ref> To date, this been the only one method able to provide evidence for the proposed non-Hund configuration at the Mo atom in Nitrogenase<ref name=":1" /> (see section [[#Nitrogenase|Nitrogeanse]]).

=== Instrumentation ===

==== A laboratory based dispersive X-ray Emission Spectrometer ====
The group of Serena DeBeer in collaboration with the group of Prof. [[Birgit Kangießer]] at [[Technical University of Berlin|TU Berlin]], developed an in-house dispersive X-ray Emission Spectroscopy (XES) setup. The setup that utilizes a laboratory X‑ray source (Metal Jet) in combination with a von Hamos full cylinder optic with [[Annealed pyrolytic graphite|Highly Annealed Pyrolytic Graphite]] (HAPG) crystal and a CCD detector. This allows obtaining spectra in the 2.4-9 keV range. Moreover, this spectrometer is an alternative to synchrotron-based beamlines for concentrated samples.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Malzer|first1=Wolfgang|last2=Grötzsch|first2=Daniel|last3=Gnewkow|first3=Richard|last4=Schlesiger|first4=Christopher|last5=Kowalewski|first5=Fabian|last6=Van Kuiken|first6=Benjamin|last7=DeBeer|first7=Serena|last8=Kanngießer|first8=Birgit|date=November 2018|title=A laboratory spectrometer for high throughput X-ray emission spectroscopy in catalysis research|journal=Review of Scientific Instruments|language=en|volume=89|issue=11|pages=113111|doi=10.1063/1.5035171|pmid=30501328|issn=0034-6748|bibcode=2018RScI...89k3111M|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==== PINK Beamline ====
The DeBeer group is also leading the development of the PINK beamline<ref name=":2" /> at the Energy Materials In-situ Laboratory<ref name=":3" /> at the [[Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin|Helmholtz Zentrum Berlin]]. Dr. Sergey Peredkov is the lead designer and instrument scientist for this project. This beamline operates in 2-10 keV energy regime, either in a “pink” beam mode with multilayer mirror or with monochromatic beam (by addition of a double crystal [[monochromator]]). The beamline is presently in a commissioning phase.
